title: How to deadlift to maximize muscle growth and minimize injury risks
summary: NH gives his cues for a safe conventional deadlift for bodybuilding: straps, bar over the whole foot, hinge into the setup, pull yourself into position with a neutral back, and lock out without leaning back. The spine is a rigid bridge while the legs and posterior chain move the weight.
claims: The deadlift is a very safe compound lift because it is positive-only; if you get hurt deadlifting you did something wrong
In the deadlift the spine is a rigid bridge connecting upper and lower body while the legs push; it is not a lower-back or spinal-torsion movement
NH has pulled heavy every two weeks for two years with no injuries or nagging pains, which he credits to technique
Bodybuilders should use straps when deadlifting; double overhand until grip fails, then straps
Mixed grip only seems stronger because it stops the bar rolling; straps do the same while avoiding biceps tears and imbalances
Forearm size won't come from deadlifts; do isolation work
Don't copy NH's exact form since segment lengths differ; apply the pointers
Set up with the bar cutting the whole foot in two (including the part behind the ankle), close to but not touching the shins
Dragging the bar up the shins means you're sitting back too much
NH prefers a closed stance; stance and grip width depend on build and preference
Reach the bar by bending knees then hinging at the hip; a clean setup negative gives a clean positive
Don't pull from the initial reach position; pull yourself into position with the bar so hamstrings are tense, shins approach but don't touch the bar
NH likes to sit back slightly then rock forward and up, but that is optional
If shoulders are too far behind the bar you're squatting the weight; the deadlift is a hip hinge, not knee flexion
Standing far from the bar and bending over turns it into a stiff-leg deadlift; the back is never parallel to the floor in a deadlift
Torso should be in between vertical and horizontal; some lower-back rounding during setup is fine, but pull with a neutral back and look forward
NH opposes a rounded thoracic spine for bodybuilders because it often leads to lumbar rounding, hips shooting up and injuries
When hips shoot up the legs lock out early and the back has to finish the lift, causing the struggle past the knees
The posterior chain from hamstrings to lower back moves the weight; everything above just maintains rigidity
Good form may mean lifting less initially but is easier to recover from and taxes the legs more
Leaning back at lockout is useless and dangerous for bodybuilders; you lock out when the joints lock, ending with a neutral spine
Don't do a slow eccentric; deadlift is positive-only, just put the bar down
exercises: straps; bar cuts whole foot in two; hinge into setup; pull into position with tense hamstrings; neutral back; look forward; lock joints, no lean-back; just put it down
grows legs and back safely when the spine stays a rigid bridge
